passage: At the village school in Kodagu, the mud by the handpump was ankle-deep after the rain. Jatin had been humming the same film song all morning, right behind Aadhya in the water line. 'Stop it,' she said. He hummed louder. So she shoved him, hard, and he sat down in the mud, his uniform brown to the waist. Some children laughed. Jatin didn't. He got up with his lip shaking. When Teacher came running, Aadhya folded her arms. 'He was annoying me all morning. He asked for it.' Teacher knelt to check Jatin's hands, then looked at her. 'He was humming. You pushed. Which of those was a choice about someone else's body?' Aadhya kicked at the mud. Teacher sent Jatin for dry clothes, kept Aadhya back to talk, and that evening told Aadhya's mother at the gate.

qa.q: Where was the mud ankle-deep?
qa.a: The mud was ankle-deep by the handpump.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya say Jatin 'asked for it'?
qa.a: She was angry at his humming, and making Jatin the cause let her feel justified instead of guilty about pushing him.

qa.q: What should Aadhya do next time someone annoys her?
qa.a: She could tell him clearly to stop, move away, or ask a teacher, rather than using her hands, and she should apologise to Jatin.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel sitting in the mud?
qa.a: He felt hurt and humiliated, his lip shaking while some children laughed and his uniform was soaked.

grounding: A child who pushed a classmate into the mud insists he was annoying and asked for it, turning the victim into the cause.

passage: At the Saturday football club in Madrid, Pablo wouldn't stop talking about his new boots. 'Real leather. Faster than yours,' he told Chidi for the fifth time on the bench. Chidi's ears went hot. When Pablo leaned over to tap Chidi's old boots, Chidi shoved him off the bench, and Pablo landed on the gravel and scraped his elbow. Coach Marta was there in seconds. 'He was being so annoying,' Chidi said before she could ask. 'Showing off all morning. He deserved it.' Coach Marta cleaned Pablo's elbow first, then sat beside Chidi. 'Pablo was annoying you. That's true. Then you pushed him. Whose choice was the push?' Chidi looked at the gravel. 'Mine,' he muttered. 'But he started it.' 'He started talking. You started pushing.' She told both boys' parents at pickup.

qa.q: What did Pablo keep talking about?
qa.a: Pablo kept talking about his new boots.

qa.q: Why did Chidi say Pablo deserved it?
qa.a: Chidi was angry and embarrassed about his old boots, and blaming Pablo's bragging let him feel justified rather than guilty about the push.

qa.q: What did Coach Marta do well?
qa.a: She cared for Pablo first, agreed the bragging was annoying, made clear that pushing was Chidi's choice, and told both families at pickup.

qa.q: How might Pablo feel after landing on the gravel?
qa.a: Pablo would likely feel hurt and shocked, and perhaps a little embarrassed about bragging, though he didn't deserve to be pushed.

grounding: A child who pushed a bragging teammate off a bench says he deserved it, making the victim the cause of his own act.

passage: In the hostel dining hall, the dinner queue was long, and Sabina slid in two places ahead of Pallavi to stand with her friend. 'Oi, back of the line,' Pallavi said. Sabina ignored her. Pallavi pushed her in the back, hard, and Sabina stumbled into the steel counter and dropped her plate with a clang. The whole hall went quiet. Sabina held her wrist, eyes wet. When the warden, Mrs Thomas, came over, Pallavi said quickly, 'She cut the line. She always does. She asked for it.' Mrs Thomas checked Sabina's wrist and sent her with a senior to the sick room. Then she turned to Pallavi. 'Cutting the line is wrong. Pushing someone into a counter is also wrong. Only one of them could break a wrist.' Pallavi's face went red. 'My office after dinner,' Mrs Thomas said. 'And I'm calling your mother tonight.'

subtype: Saying the target should have known better [Observer]
passage: On the school bus through Kandivali, the seniors in the back seat had started again: flicking Nikita's ponytail, calling her 'Miss Topper', snatching her phone and reading her messages aloud. Jatin sat two rows ahead and looked out of the window. At the stop, Nikita caught up with him, her voice tight. 'You saw. Every day this week.' Jatin shrugged, uncomfortable. 'You're too sensitive. They do it to everyone. Just toughen up and they'll get bored.' Nikita stared at him and walked off. At dinner, Jatin told his mother the story as if it were Nikita's problem. His mother put down her roti. 'They took her phone and read her messages? Every day?' 'Yeah, but—' 'That isn't her being sensitive. That's bullying. Do you have her mother's number?' subtype: Saying the target should have known better [Observer]
passage:
'You saw what they wrote under my photo,' Siddharth said at the corridor window.
Binita shifted her bag. 'Yeah. It's stupid.'
'It's every day. "Stick insect." "Lipstick boy." Forty people laughing.'
'Honestly? You make it worse. You react. If you just didn't care, they'd stop.'
'So it's my fault?'
'I didn't say that. Just... toughen up a bit. Don't be so sensitive.'
Siddharth looked at her for a long moment. 'You're my friend. You didn't say anything in the group.'
Binita opened her mouth, then closed it. Her face felt hot. 'I didn't want them to start on me,' she said finally, very quietly.
'I know.'
Silence. Then Binita said, 'Come on. Ms Ahuja's free now.'
In the counsellor's room, Ms Ahuja listened to both of them, thanked Siddharth for telling her, said none of it was his fault, and said she would speak to the class teacher and his parents before the end of the day.

qa.a: They wrote "Stick insect" and "Lipstick boy".

qa.q: Why did Binita tell Siddharth not to be so sensitive?
qa.a: Binita felt uncomfortable and scared of being targeted too, so making Siddharth responsible eased her guilt about staying silent.

qa.a: She admitted why she had stayed quiet and took Siddharth to the counsellor, who acted the same day.

subtype: Saying the target should have known better [Observer]
passage: Last year, when the girls in the hockey team started hiding Manjula's stick before every practice and calling her 'turtle' because she was slow, I told her to toughen up. Looking back, I said it because watching her made me uneasy, and it was easier if it was her fault. A week later I saw them push her stick into the drain, and I finally went to Coach Kavita. Coach listened and said, 'Lokesh, thank you for telling me.' That same afternoon she benched the three girls, spoke to Manjula alone, and called her parents. Manjula still tells people I was the one who spoke up. I don't correct her, but I remember the gate.

Gopika shook her head. 'No. Wrong question. She sat in a seat. He chose to touch her. The question is what he did, and what we do now.' She went with Tushar to the headmistress within the hour. passage: Rosa slid the letter across the café table in Berlin. The landlord was keeping her entire deposit for 'wear and tear' on a flat she had left cleaner than she found it. Selin read it and heard herself say, 'Why didn't you take photos when you moved in? Why did you let him get away with—' She stopped. Rosa's face had closed like a door. Selin put the letter down. 'Sorry. Wrong question. You didn't do anything. He decided to keep money that isn't his. That's on him.' Rosa's shoulders came down a little. 'So what do I do?' passage: In the small HR office on the third floor, Gopika finished explaining: during the late shift, her team manager had shouted at her and grabbed her arm hard enough to leave marks. Aparna, two years into HR, felt the first question rise in her throat: why did you stay late alone with him? She swallowed it. She had once asked something like that and watched a colleague stop talking. Instead she asked, 'What did he do, exactly, and when?' She wrote it down: 9:40 p.m., shouted, grabbed left arm, marks visible. 'Thank you for telling me. None of this happened because of where you were standing. He chose to do it.' Gopika's eyes filled. Aparna called the head of HR while Gopika was still in the room; the head came down within ten minutes, moved Gopika to another floor from the next day, and started the formal complaint that afternoon.

passage: The cricket ball went straight through the staffroom window at the government school, and the glass came down in a bright shower. Pankaj stood frozen with the bat. The Class 9 boys broke a whole bench in the science lab last month, and nobody said anything. And they wrote on the toilet wall. This is nothing compared to that.' The headmaster looked at the glass on the floor, then at Pankaj. 'Were the Class 9 boys holding this bat?' Pankaj looked at the bat. 'No, sir.' 'Then let's talk about this window.' Pankaj swallowed. It had seemed so small a second ago.

Tuesday. Pranav went with Papa when the glass man came. He held the new pane steady while it was fitted, and said sorry to Alka Aunty without being told. She gave him a biscuit. On the walk home he said, 'It wasn't nothing, was it?' Papa squeezed his shoulder.

passage: Seema, you say the broken bathroom mirror is tiny next to what your cousins did at Diwali. Let your Sudha Ammamma tell you about the temple lamp. When the priest came, I said, 'The big boys threw stones in the temple tank last month. This is small.' My father was standing right there. He didn't raise his voice. He said, 'The big boys will answer for the tank. You will answer for the lamp.' Then he handed me a rag. I cleaned oil for an hour, crying, and polished the lamp until it shone. I have never forgotten that sentence. Now, the mirror.

I was twenty, in my final year, and a man near the college gate wrote reports for a fee. My roommates said, 'Some people buy entire engineering degrees. A report is nothing.' So I paid. It felt small. Then came the interview for my first job. The engineer on the panel had read my report and asked me one question about the load calculations in chapter three. I didn't know them. I didn't know my own chapter. He closed the file and said, 'Whose standard are you living by?' I didn't get that job. I wrote every report myself after that, badly at first. So no, beta. Don't measure yourself against the worst person you've heard of.

qa.q: What did the engineer on the panel ask about?
qa.a: He asked about the load calculations in chapter three.

qa.q: Why did paying for the report feel small to Hemant at the time?
qa.a: Comparing it with people buying whole degrees made his shortcut seem minor, so he felt little guilt.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Hemant's choices?
qa.a: Failing to explain his own chapter in the interview and hearing 'Whose standard are you living by?', after which he wrote every report himself.

qa.q: How might the engineer on the panel have seen Hemant?
qa.a: The engineer probably saw a candidate whose report didn't match his understanding, which raised doubts about both his honesty and his skills.

grounding: An uncle recalls paying for a ghostwritten report as a student, excusing it because others bought whole degrees, and what that cost him.

subtype: Cutting corners because the rest do worse [Actor]
passage: It was 11 p.m., the hostel power had been out for two hours, and Rafiq's history essay was due at nine the next morning. He had worked three evening shifts at the call centre that week. On his phone, at nine percent, was the message from a senior: '2000 words by 7 a.m. Pay half now.' Tenzin, his roommate, looked up from his torch-lit notes. 'You're actually doing it?' 'Everyone does. Some people pay for their whole degree, Tenzin. There are colleges where you never attend a class. One essay is nothing next to that.' 'You're not them, though.' Rafiq sent the payment before he could think about it. The screen went dark as the battery died. He lay in the dark for a long time, telling himself about those other colleges, and not quite believing it.

qa.q: When was Rafiq's essay due?
qa.a: It was due at nine the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq point to people who pay for whole degrees?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and uneasy, and comparing his essay with much worse cheating made his own shortcut feel acceptable.

qa.q: What could Rafiq have done instead?
qa.a: He could have emailed the professor that night asking for a short extension, explaining the shifts and the power cut, instead of paying for someone else's work.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Rafiq's reasoning?
qa.a: Tenzin isn't persuaded and reminds Rafiq that what others do isn't his own standard.

grounding: Late at night under pressure, a student pays for a ghostwritten essay and excuses it by comparing it with people who buy whole degrees.

passage: At the end of the month, Omkar sat on the veranda of his house in Sangamner with the fuel claim form for his field visits. He had actually ridden 410 kilometres to the villages. The senior officer claimed double every month; everyone at the cooperative knew. Omkar's pen hovered over the box. A few hundred more wouldn't even be noticed. Then his four-year-old daughter Rekha climbed into his lap and pointed at the form. 'Baba, what's that?' 'A paper for the office.' 'Are you writing true things?' she asked, because that was what he always asked her about her drawings. Omkar laughed. Then he stopped laughing. If she could read this one day, would he be comfortable? He wrote 410, signed it, and let her draw a small sun in the corner of the envelope.

qa.q: How many kilometres had Omkar actually ridden?
qa.a: He had actually ridden 410 kilometres.

qa.q: What did Omkar feel when Rekha asked 'Are you writing true things?'
qa.a: He felt a jolt of uncomfortable recognition, since it was his own question to her, and it made him measure the claim against his own standard.

qa.q: Why is imagining his child reading the form a good test?
qa.a: It replaces 'the senior officer claims double' with the standard Omkar wants to live by, which resists the slide into fudging.

qa.q: What would change if Rekha one day read the form?
qa.a: She would see her Baba wrote the true figure, matching what he teaches her about telling the truth.

grounding: An adult tempted to pad a fuel claim asks whether he would be comfortable if his daughter saw it, and writes the true figure.

passage: Omar's expense report was due at midnight, and the hotel room in Toronto was quiet except for the heating. The client dinner on Tuesday was legitimate. The steak dinner alone on Wednesday, after a long day, was not. It would be so easy to write 'client follow-up'. Half the travelling team did it; he'd heard people joke about it at the airport. He typed it in. Then he thought of Wei, who sat across from him at the office, who had once driven back forty minutes to return an extra charger to a client. Omar imagined turning his screen toward Wei and saying, this one too. His face grew warm just picturing it. He deleted the line and paid for Wednesday himself. He sent the report at 11:48 and went to bed feeling oddly light.

qa.q: When was Omar's expense report due?
qa.a: It was due at midnight.

qa.q: Why did Omar's face grow warm?
qa.a: Imagining Wei seeing the false entry made Omar feel embarrassed, showing the claim didn't meet the standard he respects.

qa.q: Why was picturing Wei a good countermeasure?
qa.a: It measured the claim against a colleague whose honesty Omar admires, not against what half the team jokes about, and that stopped the slide.

qa.q: How might Wei feel if told about the deleted line?
qa.a: Wei would likely feel respect for Omar's choice, since it matches the honesty Wei shows with clients.

grounding: An adult tempted to disguise a personal dinner as a client expense imagines a respected colleague seeing it and deletes the line.

passage: In the village near Nashik, Kunal forgot to latch the goat pen on Monday evening, and the little white goat got into the neighbour's onion field. When Aai asked, Kunal said quickly, 'The wind blew the gate open.' His older brother Santosh raised an eyebrow. There hadn't been much wind. But Kunal told the same story to Aaji, then to the neighbour, then to his friend at school. Each time he added a bit: the gate banged, the goat got scared, the wind was really strong. By Thursday, when Santosh said, 'You forgot the latch,' Kunal was honestly angry. 'I didn't! I remember the wind!' He could almost hear the gate banging. Santosh just shook his head and fixed the latch himself.

qa.q: Where did the goat get into?
qa.a: The goat got into the neighbour's onion field.

qa.q: Why was Kunal honestly angry on Thursday?
qa.a: He had repeated the wind story so many times that it felt like a real memory, so being told the truth felt unfair and upsetting.

qa.q: What could help Kunal next time?
qa.a: Telling the truth right away, 'I forgot the latch', before a story gets repeated and starts to feel real.

qa.q: How does Santosh see the wind story?
qa.a: Santosh doubts it from the start, since there wasn't much wind, and he quietly fixes the latch himself.

grounding: A child tells a small fib about the goat pen and, after repeating it, comes to believe it as memory.

passage: In the apartment in São Paulo, orange juice spread across Mateo's science poster on the kitchen table. Priscila had knocked the glass while reaching for bread. When Mateo came in and yelled, she said the first thing she thought of: 'The cat jumped up.' Mateo looked at the cat, asleep on the sofa. At dinner she told Mamãe the cat story. The next day she told her friend, then her grandmother on the phone, each time adding something: the cat's paws were sticky, it knocked the glass with its tail. By the weekend, when Mateo muttered, 'You did it,' Priscila felt truly insulted. She could picture the cat's tail swishing past the glass. She wasn't lying anymore. She believed it.

qa.q: What did the juice spill on?
qa.a: It spilled on Mateo's science poster.

qa.q: Why did Priscila feel truly insulted by the weekend?
qa.a: She had repeated and decorated the cat story so often that it felt like a real memory, so Mateo's words seemed unfair.

qa.q: What could Priscila's family do to help her?
qa.a: They could calmly ask what really happened right away and praise her for owning mistakes, so a fib doesn't get repeated until it feels true.

qa.q: How does Mateo feel about the ruined poster and the story?
qa.a: Mateo is angry about the poster and frustrated that his sister keeps blaming a cat that was asleep on the sofa.

grounding: A child fibs that the cat spilled the juice and, after telling the story many times, believes it as memory.

passage: In Class 6C, Mrs Iyer collected the English homework, and Dhruv's notebook wasn't in his bag. He had left it under his bed. 'Lokesh borrowed it yesterday and didn't give it back,' he said. Lokesh, at the next desk, looked up. 'I didn't!' Dhruv told the story again at lunch, and again to his mother that evening. Each time it grew: Lokesh had asked for it at the gate, put it in his blue bag, promised to return it. On Friday, when his mother found the notebook under the bed, Dhruv stared at it, genuinely confused. 'But Lokesh had it. I remember his blue bag.' His mother sat beside him. 'Or you remember telling it.' Dhruv went quiet. The next morning he apologised to Lokesh in front of Mrs Iyer.

qa.q: Where was Dhruv's notebook really?
qa.a: It was under his bed.

qa.q: Why was Dhruv genuinely confused when the notebook turned up?
qa.a: He had repeated the story about Lokesh so many times that it felt like a memory, so the truth came as an unsettling shock.

qa.q: What did his mother's words help Dhruv understand?
qa.a: That he might remember telling the story rather than the event itself, which helped him see the excuse and apologise.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel being blamed?
qa.a: Lokesh felt shocked and wrongly accused, protesting 'I didn't!' while the story spread.

grounding: A child blames a classmate for missing homework and, after repeating the story, remembers it as true until the notebook turns up.

passage: Yogesh, you say you've read the chapter four times and you know it. That's what I said too. Let your Bhupen Dada tell you about my Class 10 physics exam in Guwahati. The night before, I turned the pages of my notes again and again. Every diagram looked familiar, every formula looked like an old friend. I went to bed thinking, I know this. Next morning the first question asked me to explain why the sky is blue, in my own words. I knew exactly where it was in my notebook, bottom of page twelve, beside a drawing of a sun. I couldn't write one sentence. I got 18 out of 50. My teacher, Mr Barua, said, 'You recognised the page, Bhupen. You never learnt the idea.' After that I closed the notebook and explained things to my little sister until she understood.

qa.q: What did Bhupen score in the physics exam?
qa.a: He got 18 out of 50.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen feel so sure he knew the chapter?
qa.a: Turning the pages again made every diagram and formula feel familiar, and that comfortable familiarity felt like understanding, so he was confident.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Bhupen studied?
qa.a: Mr Barua's words, that he recognised the page but never learnt the idea, after which he tested himself by explaining things to his sister.

qa.q: How did Mr Barua see Bhupen's result?
qa.a: He saw that Bhupen had mistaken recognising his notes for understanding, and said so plainly.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a teenager, rereading notes made him feel ready, and the exam showed familiarity was not understanding.

passage: The local train from Thane was so packed that Ramesh read his biology notes with one hand, the other gripping the overhead bar. Page after page slid past his eyes: the heart, the valves, the arrows showing blood flow. It all looked so familiar. 'Easy,' he told Sachin, squeezed in beside him. 'I've read it three times this week.' Sachin, who was drawing the heart from memory on the back of an envelope and getting it wrong, asked, 'Can you draw it?' 'I don't need to. I know it.' The unit test was at eleven. The first question said: Draw and label the human heart and explain the path of blood. Ramesh drew a lopsided oval and stared. The arrows had been right there on the page. He got 9 out of 25. Sachin, with his messy envelope, got 19.

qa.q: What did Ramesh score on the unit test?
qa.a: He got 9 out of 25.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh feel sure he knew the chapter?
qa.a: Reading the pages three times made them look familiar, and that easy recognition felt like understanding, so he was confident and saw no need to draw it.

qa.q: What could Ramesh learn from Sachin's envelope?
qa.a: Testing himself by drawing from memory, even messily, shows what he actually knows, unlike rereading.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel about his own messy practice after the result?
qa.a: Sachin would likely feel relieved and a little surprised that the imperfect drawing practice paid off.

grounding: On a crowded train, a teenager rereads notes, feels sure he knows them, and is shocked when he cannot draw the diagram in the test.

passage: The night before the history exam, Irfan lay on the sofa in their Aminabad flat, scrolling through his highlighted notes. Yellow, pink, yellow. Dates, names, causes of the revolt. 'Done,' he announced at ten. His older sister Payal looked up from her laptop. 'Tell me three causes, then.' 'I know them. They're on page six.' 'So tell me.' Irfan waved a hand. 'I've read them twice. I'm not wasting time.' He slept well. In the exam hall the next morning, the question asked him to explain two causes in his own words. He could see the pink highlighter on page six. He could not see the words. When the results came back he had 14 out of 40, and he read his answer sheet three times, shocked. He had been so sure.

qa.q: What did Irfan get on the history exam?
qa.a: He got 14 out of 40.

qa.q: Why was Irfan so shocked by his result?
qa.a: The highlighted notes had felt so familiar that he was confident he knew them, so the low mark came as a real surprise.

qa.q: What should Irfan have done when Payal asked for three causes?
qa.a: He should have tried to answer from memory, which would have shown him the gaps while there was still time to study.

qa.q: How might Payal feel when she hears the result?
qa.a: Payal might feel sympathetic but a bit exasperated, since her question could have shown him what he didn't know.

grounding: A teenager skims highlighted notes, feels sure he knows them, refuses to test himself, and is shocked by the result.
